title: A lake's incomplete memory
bodyMd:
Original natural-science exposition.

Sediment at the bottom of a lake can preserve pollen from plants that once grew nearby. In a core extracted from the lake bed, deeper layers usually formed earlier than layers above them. Researchers identify pollen grains in successive samples and use them to reconstruct changes in surrounding vegetation. The core can act like an archive, but not an evenly written one.

Some plants produce enormous quantities of wind-carried pollen; others rely on insects and release much less into the air. Pollen also travels different distances, so grains from a distant forest can reach a lake beside an open meadow. The percentage of a pollen type in a sample therefore is not a simple census of plants growing along the shore.

To constrain an interpretation, one research team compared pollen with fragments of leaves and seeds found in the same layers. Those larger fragments generally travel shorter distances. When abundant pine pollen appeared without pine needles or seeds, the researchers considered a distant source plausible. When both pollen and plant fragments increased together, local growth became a stronger explanation.

No single fragment settled the question. Water movement can transport even relatively heavy material, and preservation varies. Instead, several lines of evidence narrowed the range of reasonable histories. The team's final reconstruction described confidence separately for each interval rather than drawing one smooth boundary between forest and meadow. The untidy result was more informative than a deceptively precise line would have been.
